INDIO, California (CNN) -- For some concertgoers, the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival really kicked into action on Day Two. Festival attendees enjoy the music Saturday, Day Two of the Coachella music festival in Indio, California. Day One was leisurely and pleasant -- the weather was mild, the acts were fairly mellow and the big headliner was Paul McCartney. On Day Two, someone took the dial and turned it up a notch, as the desert sun beat down a little harder, the music pumped a little louder and the crowds who packed the VIP tent threw a little more attitude. There were the usual celebrity sightings. Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon snuck in the back just as rapper M.I.A. hit the stage, Paris Hilton took in Travis Barker and DJ AM's set in the Sahara tent and David Hasselhoff was spotted making out with a mystery lady near the restrooms. Forty-six acts performed on five stages scattered about the grassy field of the Empire Polo Club near Palm Springs, California. Massive eco-friendly art installations fashioned from scrap metal and reclaimed wood doubled as shelter from the heat, as well as mini-stages for dancers and performance artists. There was good buzz for thenewno2, an indie-pop band fronted by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison, whose vocals are reminiscent of his late father, George, but warmer, and less haunting. "It's the first festival we've ever played, and our 12th gig overall," said Harrison. "Normally with festivals, people come to check you out, stand in the back, and then move on pretty quickly, even if they like you -- but people stayed! It's the best performance we've ever had." Unfortunately Fleet Foxes was not so lucky. The Seattle,Washington, group's delicate baroque harmonies were drowned out by the world music beats of Thievery Corporation's percussion section bleeding over from the neighboring main stage, as one of their female vocalists crowd-surfed. As usual, the day's line-up was a mix of up-and-coming indie artists sprinkled with tried-and-true veteran acts. The Killers have played Coachella in both capacities. The Las Vegas, Nevada, quartet received their first invitation from festival organizers in 2004, the same year their debut album, "Hot Fuss," was released. "We played at 11:30 a.m. in a tent. It was 150 degrees out, and backstage, it smelled like horse droppings," said drummer Ronnie Vannucci, referencing the fact that there are certain consequences to holding an event on a polo field in the desert. This time, as the marquee act, The Killers enjoyed their own backstage compound decked out with a white picket fence, tablecloths and festive party lights in the shape of daisies. Palm trees gently swayed in the distance, silhouetted against the desert backdrop. You could hear the crowd going crazy for a feisty M.I.A. slotted on the main stage before The Killers. Vannucci and his three bandmates had just rolled in on their tour bus from Vegas. He spoke with CNN while warming up his hands and wrists with drumming exercises. "With festivals, you have to realize the audience is not necessarily there to see YOU. So we'll play some stuff off our new album, 'Day and Age,' and work in some songs that everybody knows, like 'Mr. Brightside' from our first album." Half an hour later, The Killers took the stage, opening their set with their latest hit, "Human." Frontman Brandon Flowers soon had the crowd singing the along to the perplexing lyrics, "Are we human, or are we dancer?" At Coachella, it doesn't matter if you're human or if you're dancer. But if you're dancer, you'll probably be relegated to one of the mini-stages inside an art installation. "The first time I heard about Coachella 10 years ago, I thought, 'That could be the cool festival here in America," said Vannucci. "It's since become a successful festival with good bands, swarms of people coming in from all over the world -- even art elements. It's strange to think we're headlining one night."

Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon slipped in through the back just as rapper M.I.A. took the stage; Paris Hilton caught Travis Barker and DJ AM’s set in the Sahara tent; and David Hasselhoff was spotted making out with a mystery woman near the restrooms.

Forty-six acts performed across five stages scattered throughout the grassy grounds of the Empire Polo Club near Palm Springs, California. Massive eco-friendly art installations, fashioned from scrap metal and reclaimed wood, doubled as shelters from the heat and mini-stages for dancers and performance artists.

There was considerable buzz surrounding thenewno2, an indie-pop band fronted by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison, whose vocals are reminiscent of those of his late father, George, but warmer and less haunting.

“It’s the first festival we’ve ever played, and our 12th gig overall,” Harrison said. “Normally with festivals, people come to check you out, stand in the back, and then move on pretty quickly, even if they like you — but people stayed! It’s the best performance we’ve ever had.”

Unfortunately, Fleet Foxes were not so lucky. The Seattle, Washington, group’s delicate baroque harmonies were drowned out by the world-music beats of Thievery Corporation’s percussion section, which bled over from the neighboring main stage as one of the group’s female vocalists crowd-surfed.

As usual, the day’s lineup featured a mix of up-and-coming indie artists and tried-and-true veteran acts. The Killers have played Coachella in both capacities.

The Las Vegas, Nevada, quartet received its first invitation from festival organizers in 2004, the same year its debut album, “Hot Fuss,” was released.

“We played at 11:30 a.m. in a tent. It was 150 degrees out, and backstage, it smelled like horse droppings,” drummer Ronnie Vannucci said, referring to the particular consequences of holding an event on a polo field in the desert.

This time, as the marquee act, The Killers enjoyed their own backstage compound, complete with a white picket fence, tablecloths, and festive party lights shaped like daisies. In the distance, palm trees swayed gently, silhouetted against the desert backdrop.

The crowd could be heard going wild for a feisty M.I.A., who was scheduled on the main stage before The Killers. Vannucci and his three bandmates had just arrived on their tour bus from Vegas. He spoke with CNN while warming up his hands and wrists with drumming exercises.

“With festivals, you have to realize the audience is not necessarily there to see YOU. So we’ll play some stuff off our new album, ‘Day and Age,’ and work in some songs that everybody knows, like ‘Mr. Brightside’ from our first album.”

Half an hour later, The Killers took the stage, opening their set with their latest hit, “Human.” Frontman Brandon Flowers soon had the crowd singing along to the perplexing lyrics: “Are we human, or are we dancer?”

At Coachella, it does not matter whether you are human or dancer. But if you are dancer, you will probably be relegated to one of the mini-stages inside an art installation.

“The first time I heard about Coachella 10 years ago, I thought, ‘That could be the cool festival here in America,’” Vannucci said. “It’s since become a successful festival with good bands, swarms of people coming in from all over the world — even art elements. It’s strange to think we’re headlining one night.”

The opening day had offered a relaxed atmosphere: comfortable temperatures, relatively subdued performers and Paul McCartney as the principal headliner. By Day Two, however, the intensity had increased. The desert heat grew stronger, the volume rose and the crowds crammed into the VIP tent displayed noticeably more attitude.

Celebrity appearances were again part of the scene. Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon slipped in through the rear entrance just as M.I.A. began performing. Paris Hilton watched Travis Barker and DJ AM in the Sahara tent, while David Hasselhoff was seen kissing an unidentified woman near the bathrooms.

Across the Empire Polo Club’s grassy grounds near Palm Springs, California, 46 acts appeared on five stages. Large environmentally conscious artworks, built from salvaged metal and reused wood, served multiple purposes: They provided relief from the sun and also functioned as small performance spaces for dancers and other artists.

One act generating favorable attention was thenewno2, an indie-pop group led by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison. Harrison’s singing recalls that of his late father, George Harrison, although his voice is warmer and not as haunting.

“This is the first festival we’ve played and only our 12th show altogether,” Harrison said. He explained that festival audiences typically stop briefly to investigate an unfamiliar band, remain toward the back and soon leave—even when they enjoy what they hear. At Coachella, however, the audience stayed. Harrison called it the band’s finest performance to date.

Fleet Foxes had a less successful experience. The Seattle, Washington, band’s subtle baroque-style vocal harmonies were overwhelmed by sound spilling over from the nearby main stage, where Thievery Corporation’s percussionists were playing world-music rhythms and one of the group’s female singers was crowd-surfing.

As is customary at Coachella, Saturday’s schedule combined emerging independent musicians with established veteran performers. The Killers had experienced the festival from both positions.

Organizers first booked the Las Vegas, Nevada, four-piece in 2004, the year the band issued its debut record, “Hot Fuss.” Drummer Ronnie Vannucci recalled that they performed in a tent at 11:30 in the morning, when the temperature felt like 150 degrees, and that the backstage area smelled of horse manure—one of the unavoidable results of staging a desert festival on a polo field.

Returning as the featured act, The Killers received far more luxurious accommodations. Their private backstage area included a white picket fence, tablecloths and celebratory lights shaped like daisies. In the distance, palm trees moved softly against the desert landscape.

Nearby, the audience could be heard reacting enthusiastically to an energetic M.I.A., whose main-stage appearance immediately preceded The Killers. Vannucci and the other three members of the band had only recently arrived by tour bus from Las Vegas. As he prepared his hands and wrists with drumming drills, he spoke to CNN about the challenge of festival performances.

Vannucci noted that musicians must remember that a festival crowd has not necessarily come specifically to see them. For that reason, he said, The Killers planned to combine tracks from their then-new album, “Day and Age,” with widely recognized songs such as “Mr. Brightside,” from their first record.

Thirty minutes later, the band began its performance with its newest hit, “Human.” Singer Brandon Flowers quickly encouraged the audience to join in on the song’s puzzling line: “Are we human, or are we dancer?”

At Coachella, whether someone is “human” or “dancer” makes little difference—although dancers are more likely to be assigned to one of the small stages incorporated into an art installation.

Vannucci said that when he first learned of Coachella a decade earlier, he believed it had the potential to become America’s cool festival. Since then, he observed, it had grown into a thriving event featuring strong bands, huge numbers of visitors from around the globe and even visual-art components. He added that it felt strange to realize The Killers were now headlining one of its nights.

**INDIO, California (CNN) —** Day Two of the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival brought rising temperatures, roaming celebrities, sprawling art installations and a packed schedule of performances to the desert Saturday, culminating in a headlining set from The Killers.

The cooler breezes of opening day gave way to more punishing afternoon heat, sending festivalgoers toward shaded tents, misting stations and any available patch of grass. By sunset, however, the Empire Polo Club grounds had filled again as fans moved between stages beneath towering sculptures and illuminated interactive artworks.

Celebrity sightings added to the festival’s anything-can-happen atmosphere. Actors, musicians and other familiar faces were spotted near the VIP areas and among the crowds, though many appeared to favor sunglasses and low-key clothing as they navigated the dusty field.

Music remained the main attraction. The day’s lineup ranged from indie rock and electronic music to hip-hop and soul, with several acts drawing audiences well beyond the edges of their tents. Fleet Foxes delivered sun-drenched harmonies, TV on the Radio brought a darker, more urgent sound, and M.I.A. turned her appearance into one of the day’s most chaotic, high-energy performances. Sets from Band of Horses, Thievery Corporation and Booker T. Jones added to the stylistic mix.

After nightfall, The Killers took control of the main stage. Frontman Brandon Flowers, dressed for spectacle despite the lingering desert warmth, led the Las Vegas band through a polished collection of anthems, including crowd favorites such as “Somebody Told Me,” “When You Were Young” and “Mr. Brightside.”

Thousands of fans sang along as lights swept across the polo grounds, giving the festival’s second day a suitably grand finale.

With another full day of music still ahead, Coachella had already delivered its familiar combination of heat, celebrity, oversized art and performances designed to be remembered long after the desert dust settled.

The second day of the 2009 Coachella festival—Saturday, April 18—moved from understated afternoon sets to a chaotic M.I.A. spectacle and a polished closing show from The Killers.

Dhani Harrison’s band, **thenewno2**, played an early set in the Mojave tent, mixing electronic textures, bluesy guitar and songs such as “Yomp” and “Another John Doe.” Although Harrison’s resemblance to his father, George Harrison, inevitably attracted attention, the performance emphasized the group rather than his lineage. Marking the occasion, Harrison told the audience, **“This is our first gig in America.”**

Later, **Fleet Foxes** provided one of the day’s quieter highlights. Their layered harmonies and pastoral songs—including material from their self-titled debut—were especially effective as the desert light began to fade. The set offered a striking contrast to the heavier, more electronic acts elsewhere on the grounds.

**Thievery Corporation** turned the main stage into a global dance party, moving through dub, reggae, bossa nova and Middle Eastern-influenced grooves. A rotating cast of singers and musicians kept the performance fluid and colorful, preparing the crowd for the evening’s most unpredictable appearance.

That came from **M.I.A.**, making one of her first major appearances after giving birth. Her set included “Bamboo Banga,” “Boyz,” “Bird Flu” and “Paper Planes,” but it was as unruly as it was energetic. Sound problems and uneven pacing occasionally disrupted the music, while dancers, flashing visuals and M.I.A.’s efforts to draw fans toward the stage created a near-riotous atmosphere. “Paper Planes,” unsurprisingly, produced the biggest response.

**The Killers** closed the night with a large-scale headlining set built around Brandon Flowers’ theatrical presence and the band’s catalogue of festival anthems. They opened with “Human” and worked through songs including “Somebody Told Me,” “Smile Like You Mean It,” “Read My Mind,” “Mr. Brightside,” “All These Things That I’ve Done” and “When You Were Young,” along with their version of Joy Division’s “Shadowplay.” Drummer Ronnie Vannucci reflected on the band’s rise from an earlier daytime Coachella appearance to the top of the bill, calling the headlining slot **“a great honor”** and adding, **“We’re just happy to be invited to the party.”**

Overall, Saturday was defined by contrasts: thenewno2’s low-key American introduction, Fleet Foxes’ precise harmonies, Thievery Corporation’s cosmopolitan rhythms, M.I.A.’s disorderly excitement and The Killers’ confident arena-rock finale.

counterfactuals.output:
At the Empire Polo Club in Indio, Coachella’s opening two days felt like separate festivals sharing the same palm-lined field. Friday unfolded at an unhurried pace, while Saturday replaced reflection with volume, movement and a headlining set that confirmed how far The Killers had climbed.

## Day One: Desert calm and veteran voices

Friday’s mood was notably mellow. Festivalgoers drifted between the Empire Polo Club’s lawns and tents rather than charging from stage to stage, settling into the dusty, sun-soaked surroundings for performances built more on atmosphere than impact. Leonard Cohen brought a hushed gravity to the evening, while Morrissey supplied his familiar blend of melancholy, wit and theatrical irritation. Franz Ferdinand and the Black Keys added sharper rhythmic edges, but the day largely belonged to songs that invited listening rather than frenzy.

Paul McCartney’s headlining appearance gave the night its emotional center. His catalog turned the enormous polo grounds into something surprisingly communal: a mass singalong shaped by Beatles standards, Wings favorites and solo material. Even at its biggest, Friday retained a warm, reflective character.

The crowd also doubled as a celebrity-watching opportunity. Reese Witherspoon and Jake Gyllenhaal were among the recognizable guests seen around the grounds, alongside Kirsten Dunst, Drew Barrymore and Justin Long. Their presence added Hollywood gloss, though the Empire Polo Club itself remained the real star: open grass, distant mountains, illuminated palms and stages scattered far enough apart to create distinct musical neighborhoods.

That sprawl also produced Coachella’s perennial frustration—scheduling conflicts. Fans had to weigh established names against emerging acts and intimate tent performances against main-stage spectacles. Leonard Cohen’s rare appearance, for example, made competing sets difficult to justify, while the overlap among indie-rock favorites forced attendees to hear partial performances or make hurried crossings through dense crowds. At Coachella, every choice comes with the awareness that something equally compelling is happening elsewhere.

## Day Two: Bigger beats and louder guitars

Saturday changed the festival’s pulse almost immediately. The relaxed wandering of Friday gave way to packed tents, aggressive bass and crowds moving with greater urgency. Fleet Foxes offered one of the day’s gentler interludes, their harmonies briefly restoring Friday’s pastoral mood, but much of the schedule leaned toward propulsion. TV on the Radio delivered dense, restless art rock; Mastodon supplied metallic force; and the dance areas grew increasingly intense as the desert cooled.

M.I.A. embodied the day’s escalation. Her set favored spectacle, booming low end and crowd participation, turning the field into a chaotic dance floor. Even when the performance felt unruly, its excess suited Saturday’s atmosphere: louder, brighter and less interested in restraint.

The scheduling dilemmas were correspondingly harsher. Indie rock, metal, electronic music and hip-hop competed across the main stage, outdoor theater and tents. Seeing a full set could mean sacrificing another major act, while trying to split the difference often meant long walks and hearing only fragments. The Empire Polo Club’s size allowed Coachella to offer several festivals at once, but it also made simultaneous must-see performances physically impossible to reconcile.

## The Killers complete their ascent

Saturday’s defining narrative belonged to The Killers. In their early Coachella years, the Las Vegas band had played an early-day tent slot—closer to a wake-up call than a coronation, with a modest audience still filtering onto the grounds. Now they returned as headliners, facing a vast nighttime crowd from the festival’s largest stage.

That progression mirrored both the band’s growth and Coachella’s role as a career-making platform. Songs that once sounded like nervy club anthems had become festival-scale standards. “Somebody Told Me,” “When You Were Young” and especially “Mr. Brightside” were no longer introductions to a promising new act; they were mass-participation moments delivered by a band fully accustomed to the size of the occasion.

Their performance also crystallized the contrast between the first two days. Friday looked backward with affection, drawing its power from legendary songwriters and collective memory. Saturday emphasized immediacy—bigger beats, harder guitars and physical release. Against the illuminated palms of the Empire Polo Club, The Killers’ rise from an early-morning tent act to Coachella headliners became the weekend’s clearest symbol of transformation.

# Coachella Day Two: Dust, Desert Art and a Mass Singalong With Brandon Flowers

**INDIO, Calif.** — By late afternoon on Coachella’s second day, the desert had settled into its familiar rhythm: bands competing with bass bleeding across the polo grounds, sunburned crowds migrating between tents and enormous art installations, and the San Jacinto Mountains looming beyond the stages like an impossibly polished backdrop.

The festival, held outside Palm Springs, felt busiest in the corridors between performances. Friends formed human chains to keep from being separated. Barefoot dancers threaded past blankets spread across the grass, while veteran festivalgoers searched for shade and newcomers stopped repeatedly to photograph the sculptures rising above the field.

Many of those installations doubled as environmental statements. Structures assembled from reclaimed or low-impact materials offered flashes of color against the sand and grass, while decorated recycling stations tried to make waste sorting part of the spectacle. The eco-conscious touches did not disguise the scale of the event—cups, food trays and water bottles still accumulated quickly—but they gave the grounds the feel of a temporary desert city attempting to reckon with its own footprint.

Musically, Saturday moved between indie discovery and institutional confidence. Younger acts drew crowds eager to hear blog favorites in the open air, their intimate songs sometimes transformed—and occasionally overwhelmed—by the size of the setting. Elsewhere, veteran performers demonstrated the value of pacing: fewer theatrics, tighter arrangements and an ease that came from knowing exactly how long to hold a groove.

That contrast defined much of the day. In the tents, audiences packed close for sets that felt sweaty and immediate. At the larger stages, guitars and synthesizers rolled across thousands of people, with choruses traveling farther than verses and familiar songs producing sudden surges toward the front.

Backstage, the festival was less bohemian than logistical. Golf carts zipped along fenced lanes. Crew members pushed equipment cases through the dust, publicists checked schedules, and artists moved between shaded compounds and stages with little time to spare. From behind the performance areas, the roar of the audience arrived in waves—loudest when a recognizable opening riff escaped the speakers.

The day’s defining communal moment came with Brandon Flowers and “Human.” Dressed with the polished showmanship that has long distinguished him from more deliberately rumpled indie frontmen, Flowers treated the song less like a performance than a piece of mass participation.

He guided the audience into its central refrain, letting thousands of voices carry the question back toward the stage: **“Are we human, or are we dancer?”**

Whatever debate the lyric once inspired disappeared in the moment. Across the field, people raised their arms, climbed onto shoulders and sang with the earnestness that only a festival crowd can make seem natural. Flowers stepped back enough to hear the response, then drove the band forward again.

By nightfall, the heat had loosened its grip, illuminated art glowed across the grounds, and the crowd’s daytime sprawl condensed into dense pockets around the headliners. Day Two had offered Coachella in miniature: environmental aspiration beside conspicuous consumption, emerging acts beside seasoned performers, backstage machinery beside front-of-stage abandon.

And for a few minutes during “Human,” the vast, unruly festival became a single choir in the desert.

## The Killers complete their Coachella climb

Five years after arriving at Coachella as a fast-rising Las Vegas band in 2004, The Killers returned in 2009 to headline the festival’s main stage—a promotion that underscored how quickly songs such as “Mr. Brightside,” “Somebody Told Me” and “All These Things That I’ve Done” had moved from indie-club favorites to mass singalongs.

Drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr. said festivals present a different test from a normal Killers concert. A band cannot assume everyone in front of it is a fan: many people are waiting for another act, sampling the headliner or simply attending the larger event. Festival crowds therefore have to be won over, he explained, and can be less predictable—and less forgiving—than an audience that bought tickets specifically to see the group.

Behind the main stage, the band occupied a small compound of trailers and an outdoor gathering area, giving members, relatives, friends and crew somewhere to escape the heat and commotion. Despite the headliner amenities, the atmosphere was more functional and familial than decadent: a temporary home base where the band could eat, visit and prepare while the festival continued nearby.

The planned performance was built like a career survey. The Killers intended to begin with “Human,” then move through material from *Hot Fuss*, *Sam’s Town* and *Day & Age*. The set included “This Is Your Life,” “Somebody Told Me,” “For Reasons Unknown,” “Smile Like You Mean It,” “Spaceman,” “A Dustland Fairytale,” “Read My Mind,” “Mr. Brightside” and their Joy Division cover “Shadowplay.” The encore was designed for maximum impact: “Bones,” “Jenny Was a Friend of Mine” and “When You Were Young,” with “All These Things That I’ve Done” providing another of the night’s largest communal choruses.

Their appearance capped a crowded Saturday marked by sharply contrasting performances. Fleet Foxes and Band of Horses supplied sweeping harmonies and guitar music, while TV on the Radio brought a more experimental edge. The day’s most unruly scene belonged to M.I.A., whose set drew an enormous crowd and spilled into near-chaos as fans surged toward—and onto—the stage. The Chemical Brothers kept the dance tents active after the main-stage rock spectacle.

For The Killers, however, the day’s lasting image was the scale of the journey: from a relatively low position on the 2004 bill to standing beneath the lights as Coachella headliners, facing the kind of mixed festival audience Vannucci believed had to be earned one song at a time.
